Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Sudden painless left-arm paralysis with concurrent left facial paresthesia, mild dysarthria, and swallowing difficulty beginning on waking (~1 h earlier).  
• Vascular risk factors: T2DM, hypertension, prior smoking, alcohol use.  
• No trauma, headache, limb discoloration, or leg involvement.

Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and DDx)  
1. Acute ischemic stroke – High likelihood given abrupt focal neurological deficit pattern and risk profile.  
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage – Moderate likelihood; identical presentation possible in hypertensive patient, though absence of headache or reduced consciousness reduces probability.  
3. Transient ischemic attack – Moderate but decreasing likelihood as deficits persist and appear to worsen.

Working diagnosis: Suspected acute cerebrovascular event (likely ischemic stroke) – time of onset uncertain but within estimated therapeutic window.

Immediate plan (implemented during call)  
• Emergency ambulance arranged to convey patient to hospital for stroke team assessment and potential reperfusion therapy.  
• Advice to unlock front door, wait seated in hallway; clinician remained on line until paramedics arrived.  
• No medications administered; no additional in-office investigations possible in telehealth context.

Management Plan

- Immediate transfer to emergency department via ambulance (executed).  
- Hospital evaluation to include brain imaging (CT/MRI), neurological assessment, and consideration of thrombolysis/thrombectomy per stroke protocol.  
- In-hospital management of blood pressure, glucose, and secondary prevention measures anticipated.  
- Education: advised on urgency; instructions for safe access to ambulance.  
- Follow-up with primary care post-discharge for ongoing stroke prevention and chronic disease management (HTN, T2DM).

1. Acute ischemic stroke – High likelihood: sudden unilateral motor deficit with facial/speech involvement in patient with vascular risk factors.  
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage – Moderate likelihood: hypertensive patient with abrupt deficit; lacks headache or altered consciousness.  
3. Transient ischemic attack – Moderate likelihood: similar presentation but deficits have not resolved.
